output.answer:
`weave.init()` sets up Weave in your Python process: it signs in to Weights & Biases and starts tracing so your data goes to a project [S3]. Pass either `"team-name/project-name"` to log to a specific team, or just `"project-name"` to log to your default team or entity [S1].

**What `weave.init` does**
- It signs in to Weights & Biases and sets up where traces are sent. In the agent quickstart, it configures the exporter that sends agent spans to the **Agents** view [S3].
- If the project doesn't exist on your team yet, Weave creates it the first time you write to it [S3].
- After you call it, Weave starts capturing traces for supported libraries, such as Groq, which you then use as normal [S4].
- It returns a client object with `entity` and `project` attributes, which you can use later, for example to build links [S2].

**Which project string to pass**
- `"my-project"`: logs to your default team or entity [S1].
- `"my-team/my-project"`: logs to a specific team [S1]. Use this form when you belong to more than one team and need to choose where traces go.

```python
import weave

# Pass the string as the first argument. Replace the placeholders with your names.
client = weave.init("my-team/my-project")   # or weave.init("my-project")
print(client.entity, client.project)
```

Call it near the start of your script, before running the code you want to trace [S1]. In the docs' examples, the string is the first argument [S3]. Some integration pages pass it by name instead, but they use different names: `project_name=` [S4] and `project=` [S1]. Passing it as the first argument avoids that mismatch.

# Quickstart: Set up custom agent observability

> Trace a multi-turn agent with the Weave SDK. Conversations, turns, LLM calls, and tool calls render in the Agents view of your project.

> [!TIP]
>
> **This workflow is also available in CoreWeave Agent Lens.** Agent Lens is the Forge experience built for tracing, monitoring, and analyzing AI agents, with automated insights into agent failures and user intents. It uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave, so the traces you already send appear there with nothing to migrate.
> [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/get-started/custom-agents.md).

[Try in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/github/wandb/examples/blob/main/colabs/weave/custom-agents-quickstart.ipynb) · [GitHub source](https://github.com/wandb/examples/blob/main/colabs/weave/custom-agents-quickstart.ipynb)

The Weave SDK lets you trace agents built with popular SDKs or custom harnesses. This quickstart shows you how to manually integrate Weave into a custom-built multi-turn agent to emit and capture OpenTelemetry spans. For conceptual understanding about Weave for agents, see [Trace your agents](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/trace-agents.md).

If you're looking to integrate Weave with SDKs or harnesses such as the Claude Agent SDK or Codex, see [Choose an agent integration](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/agent-integration-quickstart.md). Weave autopatches into several agent-building SDKs and agent harnesses for quick integration.

sources.title: Verdict
sources.heading: Getting started
sources.text:
## Getting started

To enable Weave tracing for your Verdict pipelines, call `weave.init(project=...)` at the beginning of your script. Use the `project` argument to log to a specific Weights & Biases Team name with `team-name/project-name`, or pass `project-name` to log to your default team or entity.

```python lines {7} theme={"system"}
import weave
from verdict import Pipeline
from verdict.common.judge import JudgeUnit
from verdict.schema import Schema

# Initialize Weave with your project name
weave.init("verdict_demo")

# Create a simple evaluation pipeline
pipeline = Pipeline()
pipeline = pipeline >> JudgeUnit().prompt("Rate the quality of this text: {source.text}")

# Create sample data
data = Schema.of(text="This is a sample text for evaluation.")

# Run the pipeline - Weave traces this automatically
output = pipeline.run(data)

print(output)
```

# Verdict

> Use Verdict evaluation framework with Weave to trace and monitor your LLM evaluation pipelines

[GitHub source](https://github.com/wandb/examples/blob/master/weave/docs/quickstart_verdict.ipynb)

Weave is designed to track and log all calls made through the [Verdict Python library](https://verdict.haizelabs.com/docs/) automatically.

When working with AI evaluation pipelines, debugging matters. Whether a pipeline step fails, outputs are unexpected, or nested operations create confusion, pinpointing issues can be hard. Verdict applications often consist of multiple pipeline steps, judges, and transformations, so it helps to understand the inner workings of your evaluation workflows.

Weave streamlines this process by automatically capturing traces for your [Verdict](https://verdict.readthedocs.io/) applications. This lets you monitor and analyze your pipeline's performance to debug and optimize your AI evaluation workflows.

sources.title: Groq
sources.heading: Tracing
sources.text:
## Tracing

It's important to store traces of language model applications in a central location, both during development and in production. These traces can help you debug your application and serve as a dataset to improve it.

Weave automatically captures traces for [Groq](https://groq.com/). To start tracking, call `weave.init(project_name="<your-wandb-project-name>")` and use the library as normal. Replace values enclosed in `<>` with your own.

```python lines theme={"system"}
import os
import weave
from groq import Groq

weave.init(project_name="groq-project")

client = Groq(
    api_key=os.environ.get("GROQ_API_KEY"),
)
chat_completion = client.chat.completions.create(
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "Explain the importance of fast language models",
        }
    ],
    model="llama3-8b-8192",
)
```

| ![Groq Weave dashboard with tracked LLM calls, performance metrics, and trace information](https://mintcdn.com/coreweave-dbfa0e8d/3Dv_sw2eg8feUJlx/products/wandb/weave/_media/groq_weave_dasboard.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=3Dv_sw2eg8feUJlx\&q=85\&s=25746a7310d4cab0ee36dad1045b6cc7) |
| - |
| Weave now tracks and logs all LLM calls made through the Groq library. You can view the traces in the Weave web interface. |

# Groq

> Track and monitor Groq LPU inference with Weave, capturing model calls, performance metrics, and function chains for LLM applications.

[Try in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/github/wandb/examples/blob/master/weave/docs/quickstart_groq.ipynb)

> [!NOTE]
>
> Do you want to experiment with Groq models on Weave without any setup? Try the [LLM Playground](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tools/playground.md).

[Groq](https://groq.com/) is an AI infrastructure company that delivers fast AI inference. The LPU Inference Engine by Groq is a hardware and software platform built for compute speed, quality, and energy efficiency. Weave automatically tracks and logs Groq chat completion calls.

This page explains how to use Weave to trace Groq chat completion calls, wrap your own functions as Weave ops, and organize your experiments using `Model` objects.

sources.heading: Link to a conversation from your app
sources.text:
## Link to a conversation from your app

To deep-link from your own UI to a conversation in the Weave Agents view, build the URL from your entity, project, and the conversation id. `weave.init()` returns a client that carries `entity` and `project`, and `start_conversation` exposes `conversation_id`.

```python lines Python theme={"system"}
from weave.trace.urls import agent_conversation_path

client = weave.init(f"{TEAM}/{PROJECT}")

with weave.start_conversation(agent_name="research-bot") as conversation:
    # ... run turns ...
    url = agent_conversation_path(
        client.entity, client.project, conversation.conversation_id
    )
    print(f"View this conversation at {url}")
```

```plaintext TypeScript lines theme={"system"}
This feature is not available in TypeScript.
```

> Track and monitor Groq LPU inference with Weave, capturing model calls, performance metrics, and function chains for LLM applications.

[Try in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/github/wandb/examples/blob/master/weave/docs/quickstart_groq.ipynb)

> [!NOTE]
>
> Do you want to experiment with Groq models on Weave without any setup? Try the [LLM Playground](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tools/playground.md).

[Groq](https://groq.com/) is an AI infrastructure company that delivers fast AI inference. The LPU Inference Engine by Groq is a hardware and software platform built for compute speed, quality, and energy efficiency. Weave automatically tracks and logs Groq chat completion calls.

This page explains how to use Weave to trace Groq chat completion calls, wrap your own functions as Weave ops, and organize your experiments using `Model` objects.

results.snippet:
## Link to a conversation from your app

To deep-link from your own UI to a conversation in the Weave Agents view, build the URL from your entity, project, and the conversation id. `weave.init()` returns a client that carries `entity` and `project`, and `start_conversation` exposes `conversation_id`.

```python lines Python theme={"system"}
from weave.trace.urls import agent_conversation_path

client = weave.init(f"{TEAM}/{PROJECT}")

with weave.start_conversation(agent_name="research-bot") as conversation:
    # ... run turns ...
    url = agent_conversation_path(
        client.entity, client.project, conversation.conversation_id
    )
    print(f"View this conversation at {url}")
```

results.snippet:
## Getting started

To enable Weave tracing for your Verdict pipelines, call `weave.init(project=...)` at the beginning of your script. Use the `project` argument to log to a specific Weights & Biases Team name with `team-name/project-name`, or pass `project-name` to log to your default team or entity.

```python lines {7} theme={"system"}
import weave
from verdict import Pipeline
from verdict.common.judge import JudgeUnit
from verdict.schema import Schema

# Initialize Weave with your project name
weave.init("verdict_demo")

# Create a simple evaluation pipeline
pipeline = Pipeline()
pipeline = pipeline >> JudgeUnit().prompt("Rate the quality of this text: {source.text}")

# Create sample data
data = Schema.of(text="This is a sample text for evaluation.")

# Run the pipeline - Weave traces this automatically
output = pipeline.run(data)

print(output)
```

results.title: Trace your code
results.heading: Track custom functions
results.snippet:
## Track custom functions

LLM applications often have additional logic, such as pre-processing and post-processing, prompts, and more, that you want to track. Use this approach when you want Weave to capture your own functions alongside the LLM calls it traces automatically.

**Python**

Weave lets you manually track these Calls using the [`@weave.op`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/reference/python-sdk#function-op) decorator. For example:

```python lines theme={"system"}
import weave

# Initialize Weave Tracing
weave.init('intro-example')

# Decorate your function
@weave.op
def my_function(name: str):
    return f"Hello, {name}!"

# Call your function -- Weave will automatically track inputs and outputs
print(my_function("World"))
```

You can also track [methods on classes](#track-class-and-object-methods).

**TypeScript**

Weave lets you manually track these Calls by wrapping your function with [`weave.op`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/reference/typescript-sdk/functions/op). For example:

```typescript twoslash lines theme={"system"}
// @noErr

results.title: Reference media in your own bucket (BYOB) using Weave Op
results.heading: Log a media reference using Weave Op function tracing
results.snippet:
## Log a media reference using Weave Op function tracing

Log the URI as a string value in a trace. Any string field whose value is a bucket URI renders. No content annotation is needed because the bytes stay in your bucket. The following example Op captions images that already live in your bucket and logs each URI alongside its caption. Replace `[YOUR-TEAM]`, `[YOUR-PROJECT]`, and `[YOUR-BUCKET]` with your own values.

> [!TIP]
>
> If you're adding reference media to an agentic application, see [Reference media in agent spans](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/agents-byob-references.md) instead.

**Python**

```python lines theme={"system"}
import weave

weave.init("[YOUR-TEAM]/[YOUR-PROJECT]")

@weave.op
def caption_image(image_uri: str) -> dict:
    caption = my_captioner(image_uri)  # Your model or API call.
    # image_uri renders inline from its value; the field name is arbitrary
    # and the extension (.png here) decides image vs video.
    return {"image": image_uri, "caption": caption}

caption_image("s3://[YOUR-BUCKET]/photos/cat.png")
```

results.title: Instructor
results.heading: Tracing
results.snippet:
## Tracing

It's important to store traces of language model applications in a central location, both during development and in production. These traces can be useful for debugging, and as a dataset that will help you improve your application.

Weave automatically captures traces for [Instructor](https://python.useinstructor.com/). To start tracking, call `weave.init(project_name="[YOUR-WANDB-PROJECT-NAME]")` and use the library as normal.

```python lines theme={"system"}
import instructor
import weave
from pydantic import BaseModel
from openai import OpenAI


# Define your desired output structure
class UserInfo(BaseModel):
    user_name: str
    age: int

# Initialize Weave
weave.init(project_name="instructor-test")

# Patch the OpenAI client
client = instructor.from_openai(OpenAI())

# Extract structured data from natural language
user_info = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-3.5-turbo",
    response_model=UserInfo,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "John Doe is 30 years old."}],
)
```

results.heading: Manual Call tracking
results.snippet:
## Manual Call tracking

If neither automatic integration nor the `weave.op` decorator fits your workflow, you can manually create Calls using the API directly. This approach gives you full control over when a Call starts and ends, at the cost of more boilerplate.

**Python**

```python lines theme={"system"}
import weave

# Initialize Weave Tracing
client = weave.init('intro-example')

def my_function(name: str):
    # Start a Call
    call = client.create_call(op="my_function", inputs={"name": name})

    # ... your function code ...

    # End a Call
    client.finish_call(call, output="Hello, World!")

# Call your function
print(my_function("World"))
```

**TypeScript**

```text theme={"system"}
This feature is not available in the TypeScript SDK yet.
```

**HTTP API**

* Start a Call: [POST `/call/start`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/reference/service-api/calls/call-start).
* End a Call: [POST `/call/end`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/reference/service-api/calls/call-end).

## Tracing

It's important to store traces of language model applications in a central location, both during development and in production. These traces can help you debug your application and serve as a dataset to improve it.

Weave automatically captures traces for [Groq](https://groq.com/). To start tracking, call `weave.init(project_name="<your-wandb-project-name>")` and use the library as normal. Replace values enclosed in `<>` with your own.

```python lines theme={"system"}
import os
import weave
from groq import Groq

weave.init(project_name="groq-project")

client = Groq(
    api_key=os.environ.get("GROQ_API_KEY"),
)
chat_completion = client.chat.completions.create(
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "Explain the importance of fast language models",
        }
    ],
    model="llama3-8b-8192",
)
```

## Traces

This section shows you how to enable automatic tracing of DSPy calls in Weave. Store traces of language model applications in a central location, both during development and in production. These traces are useful for debugging and as a dataset that helps you improve your application.

Weave automatically captures traces for [DSPy](https://dspy.ai). To start tracking, call `weave.init(project_name="[YOUR-WANDB-PROJECT-NAME]")` and use the library as normal. Replace `[YOUR-OPENAI-API-KEY]` with your OpenAI API key and `[YOUR-WANDB-PROJECT-NAME]` with your Weights & Biases project name.

```python lines theme={"system"}
import os
import dspy
import weave

os.environ["OPENAI_API_KEY"] = "[YOUR-OPENAI-API-KEY]"

weave.init(project_name="[YOUR-WANDB-PROJECT-NAME]")

lm = dspy.LM('openai/gpt-4o-mini')
dspy.configure(lm=lm)
classify = dspy.Predict("sentence -> sentiment")
classify(sentence="it's a charming and often affecting journey.")
```

`weave.init()` sets up Weave in your Python process: it signs in to Weights & Biases and starts tracing so your data goes to a project [S3]. Pass either `"team-name/project-name"` to log to a specific team, or just `"project-name"` to log to your default team or entity [S1].

**What `weave.init` does**
- It signs in to Weights & Biases and sets up where traces are sent. In the agent quickstart, it configures the exporter that sends agent spans to the **Agents** view [S3].
- If the project doesn't exist on your team yet, Weave creates it the first time you write to it [S3].
- After you call it, Weave starts capturing traces for supported libraries, such as Groq, which you then use as normal [S4].
- It returns a client object with `entity` and `project` attributes, which you can use later, for example to build links [S2].

**Which project string to pass**
- `"my-project"`: logs to your default team or entity [S1].
- `"my-team/my-project"`: logs to a specific team [S1]. Use this form when you belong to more than one team and need to choose where traces go.

```python
import weave

# Pass the string as the first argument. Replace the placeholders with your names.
client = weave.init("my-team/my-project")   # or weave.init("my-project")
print(client.entity, client.project)
```

Call it near the start of your script, before running the code you want to trace [S1]. In the docs' examples, the string is the first argument [S3]. Some integration pages pass it by name instead, but they use different names: `project_name=` [S4] and `project=` [S1]. Passing it as the first argument avoids that mismatch.
